tldr: 🤖 Stripe finalizes a reported $7B+ deal for AI model gateway OpenRouter.
🌍 The 60-day US–Iran ceasefire MOU lapses with Hormuz still effectively shut.
📉 China's July output, retail sales and investment all miss forecasts.
🏥 AstraZeneca kills its Phase III volrustomig lung cancer trial.
🃏 Kushner meets Netanyahu after rare direct talks with Hamas in Egypt.
🃏 Japan's Q2 GDP grows 1.1% annualized against a 2% forecast.
🃏 US prescription drug prices post their steepest annual drop since 1963.
🃏 Guardian: Microsoft has ~2.2M AI chips installed after ~$280B of spending.
🔴 BBC asks a Florida court to subpoena Don Jr., Ivanka and Kushner.
💻 Researchers publish a full-kernel Unisoc phone exploit with no vendor fix.

items.headline: Stripe finalizes a reported $7 billion-plus purchase of OpenRouter
items.body: Bloomberg reported on August 16 that Stripe has finalized an agreement to buy OpenRouter, the New York startup whose single API routes developer traffic across more than 400 AI models. OpenRouter says it serves 8 million developers; it raised a $113 million Series B at a reported $1.3 billion valuation only months ago, making this roughly a 5x markup. The Wall Street Journal had earlier reported talks near $10 billion. Stripe told TechCrunch it does not comment on rumors, so the deal is not company-confirmed.
items.plain: Stripe is the company that quietly handles the credit-card payments for a huge chunk of the internet. It's buying a company that works like a universal remote for AI: instead of a programmer signing up separately with 400 different AI companies, they plug into OpenRouter once and can reach all of them. Stripe is paying over $7 billion to own that middle position — because whoever sits in the middle gets to take a small cut of everything that passes through.
items.why: The premium is being paid for the routing and metering layer rather than the models, which is where margin accrues once frontier model prices keep falling.

items.headline: The US–Iran ceasefire memorandum expires with no extension and the strait still closed
items.body: The 60-day Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed on June 17 lapsed on August 16–17 with negotiations at a standstill; a senior White House official described them to Politico as "static." Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Iran has "not made a decision to restart negotiations with the United States," and Tehran maintains the 60-day clock never started. Kpler recorded only three ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, a new low for a waterway that carried about a fifth of world oil and gas before the February 28 US–Israeli strikes. Brent traded near $88–91.
items.plain: Back in June, the US and Iran signed a deal to stop shooting at each other for 60 days. That clock just ran out and nobody renewed it — the two sides aren't even really talking. Meanwhile the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that about a fifth of the world's oil normally travels through, is basically shut: only three ships went through on Sunday. With no agreement left on paper, there's nothing formally stopping the fighting from restarting, and oil prices are sitting high because of it.
items.why: With no legal framework left, the next move is military rather than diplomatic, and the oil market is pricing a supply outage that the EIA does not expect to normalize until early 2027.

items.headline: China's July data misses across every major indicator
items.body: Industrial output rose 4.5% year on year, below the 4.8% consensus and down from 5.3% in June. Retail sales grew just 0.6% against a 1.5% Reuters poll forecast. Urban fixed-asset investment for January–July fell 6.7% year on year, worse than the 6% decline expected and steeper than the 5.7% drop through the first half. New home prices extended their declines.
items.plain: Every major scoreboard for China's economy came in worse than experts predicted. Factories made less than expected, shoppers spent barely anything more than last year, and — the important one — businesses spent 6.7% less on new buildings and equipment than they did a year ago. That last number is the tell: when companies stop investing in their own future, it usually means they don't believe things are about to get better.
items.why: A 6.7% investment contraction is not a soft patch in demand but a balance-sheet retreat, which pushes Beijing toward stimulus it has so far declined to deliver.

items.headline: AstraZeneca halts its Phase III volrustomig trial in first-line lung cancer
items.body: AstraZeneca said on August 17 it is discontinuing eVOLVE-Lung02, which tested the PD-1/CTLA-4 bispecific volrustomig plus chemotherapy against Merck's Keytruda plus chemotherapy in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with PD-L1 expression below 50%. A planned interim review found volrustomig unlikely to meet either primary endpoint, progression-free survival or overall survival, with no unexpected safety findings. Phase III programs in cervical cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and mesothelioma continue.
items.plain: AstraZeneca was testing a new cancer drug head-to-head against Keytruda, the drug that's currently the go-to treatment for this kind of lung cancer. Partway through the study, the independent scientists who monitor the results took a look and concluded the new drug wasn't going to beat Keytruda at helping people live longer — so they stopped the trial early rather than keep going. Nobody was hurt by the drug; it just didn't work well enough. AstraZeneca is still testing it against other cancers.
items.why: Keytruda's patent cliff arrives in 2028 and this was one of the credible attempts to displace it in the largest oncology indication, so the incumbent franchise gets a longer runway than expected.

items.headline: Kushner meets Netanyahu after rare direct talks with Hamas in Egypt
items.body: Jared Kushner held a roughly two-hour meeting on Sunday in El-Alamein, Egypt with a Hamas delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya, then met Netanyahu for hours on Monday. At issue is a 15-point US road map under which Hamas disarms and Israel withdraws; Hamas endorsed it two weeks ago and Netanyahu has refused, insisting the group be "genuinely disarmed." Al-Hayya demanded Israel halt attacks and pull back to the "yellow line" first. The foreign ministers of Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia and Pakistan issued a joint statement blaming Israel for the impasse.
items.plain: Jared Kushner — Trump's son-in-law, acting as a US negotiator — sat down face to face with Hamas in Egypt for about two hours, then met Israel's prime minister the next day. The deal on the table is basically a trade: Hamas gives up its weapons, Israel pulls its troops out. Hamas already said yes to it two weeks ago; Israel is the one saying no. The genuinely unusual part is the US talking to Hamas directly at all — normally another country passes messages between them — and it means the US and Israel are now openly disagreeing in public.
items.why: Washington is now negotiating directly with Hamas against Israeli objections, which inverts the usual mediation structure and puts US and Israeli positions publicly at odds.

items.headline: Japan's economy grew half as fast as forecast in the second quarter
items.body: Q2 GDP expanded 1.1% on an annualized basis against a 2% consensus, or 0.3% quarter on quarter versus 0.5% expected. Private consumption, more than half of output, was effectively flat at an annualized -0.1%. Business investment contracted 1.2% against expectations of a 0.4% gain. The Bank of Japan nudged its fiscal 2026 growth outlook to 0.6% from 0.5% while citing high crude prices from the Middle East conflict.
items.plain: Japan's economy did grow — but only about half as much as economists expected. Two things went wrong: regular people didn't increase their spending at all, and businesses actually cut back on investing instead of increasing it. This matters because Japan's central bank has been saying it wants proof the economy is genuinely strong before it raises interest rates. This is the opposite of proof, so that rate hike gets pushed further away.
items.why: Falling capex and flat consumption remove the domestic-demand evidence the BOJ has said it needs, pushing the next rate hike further out and keeping downward pressure on the yen.

items.headline: US prescription drug prices post their steepest annual decline since 1963
items.body: Prescription drug prices fell 3.1% from July 2025, the largest year-over-year drop since March 1963. Prices have not risen in any month of 2026 and have fallen in five of the last six. The administration has signed most-favored-nation pricing deals with 17 large drugmakers covering roughly 86% of the branded market, including Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Regeneron; Medicare's first 10 negotiated prices also took effect January 1. Analysts disagree on how much of the decline each mechanism explains.
items.plain: Prescription drugs in the US got 3.1% cheaper than a year ago — the biggest one-year drop since 1963, which is genuinely rare. It happened because the government pressured 17 big drug companies into pricing agreements covering most brand-name medicines. Here's the catch worth noticing: the price printed on the medicine went down, but health insurance premiums are still set to jump around 15% next year. So the savings are real, but they're getting absorbed somewhere between the drug company and your household rather than showing up in what families actually pay.
items.why: List prices are falling while ACA marketplace insurers propose a median 15% premium increase for 2027, so the savings are landing somewhere other than household premiums.

items.headline: Guardian investigation puts Microsoft's installed AI chip count near 2.2 million
items.body: Internal documents reviewed by The Guardian indicate Microsoft has roughly 2.2 million AI accelerators installed worldwide, after spending about $280 billion since 2022 on land, buildings and compute. The company had targeted 1.8 million chips installed by end-2024. Satya Nadella has previously said the binding constraint is power and finished data center shells rather than GPU supply. Microsoft disputed the Guardian's calculations without specifying which figures it considers wrong. This is single-outlet investigative reporting.
items.plain: Leaked internal documents suggest Microsoft has spent roughly $280 billion building AI data centers, but only has about 2.2 million AI chips actually plugged in and running — behind where it hoped to be two years ago. The surprising reason isn't that chips are hard to buy. It's that you can't use a chip until you've built the building to put it in and connected enough electricity to power it, and construction and power lines move slowly. Microsoft says the Guardian's math is wrong but won't say which numbers. Only one outlet has this story so far, so treat it as credible but unconfirmed.
items.why: If the largest buyer's capex is converting to live compute this slowly, the sector's revenue forecasts are gated by substations and construction crews, not chip allocation.

items.headline: BBC asks a Florida court to subpoena Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner
items.body: In a motion filed Friday, August 14, the BBC asked a Florida federal court to authorize subpoenas for testimony and records from the president's two eldest children and his son-in-law, in its defense against Trump's $10 billion defamation suit over the documentary "Trump: A Second Chance?" The filing states the three "have personal knowledge and likely have possession, custody, or control of records" relevant to the case, that Donald Jr. and Ivanka were present when Trump revised and delivered his January 6, 2021 speech, and that Kushner drafted a proposed statement condemning violence. BBC lawyers wrote they were previously blocked from serving Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their Florida home by law enforcement and redirected to the Secret Service. The motion is pending; no ruling has issued.
items.plain: Trump is suing the BBC for $10 billion, claiming a documentary lied about him. But when you sue someone, they get to gather evidence to defend themselves — and the BBC is now asking a judge for permission to force Don Jr., Ivanka, and Jared Kushner to testify under oath and hand over their records. The BBC specifically wants to ask about January 6th, 2021, since it says Don Jr. and Ivanka were in the room while Trump edited and gave his speech that day. The irony is the point: by choosing to sue, Trump created the one situation where his own family might have to answer those questions under oath — something years of congressional investigations never managed. The judge hasn't decided yet.
items.why: Trump's own libel suit is what opens the door to sworn family testimony about January 6 that no congressional subpoena ever compelled.

items.headline: Researchers publish a full-kernel Unisoc phone exploit the chipmaker has not answered
items.body: SSD Secure Disclosure published an advisory on August 17 completing a two-stage chain that achieves full Android kernel access on devices using Unisoc modem firmware, starting from a malformed SIP video call disclosed in March. The second stage bypasses the ARM memory protection unit, making the entire 32-bit address space readable, writable and executable from modem context. Exploitation requires the attacker to run a private 4G network and the victim to answer the call. "We have tried to reach out to the vendor through multiple channels (email and LinkedIn) but have not been able to receive any response," the researchers wrote. No patch exists.
items.plain: Security researchers figured out how to completely take over certain cheap Android phones by attacking the part of the chip that handles phone calls — the way in is a deliberately broken video call. It's not something that can happen to you casually: the attacker has to set up their own fake cell tower nearby, and you have to actually answer the call. The real problem is the ending. The researchers tried repeatedly to warn the chipmaker by email and LinkedIn and never got a single reply, so they published it with no fix available. These chips sit inside budget phones used by a lot of people across South Asia, Africa and Latin America, who now have no way to patch it.
items.why: Unisoc ships the silicon in low-cost handsets across South Asia, Africa and Latin America, a population with no realistic patch path when the vendor simply does not reply.
